findings.quote: If a double bond, triple bond or functional group is present, the parent must contain it. A longer chain that leaves it out is the wrong parent.
findings.problem: This is stated as an absolute IUPAC rule, and it fails. Under the current IUPAC recommendations (2013), the longest chain comes first when choosing the principal chain, and unsaturation is only a later tiebreaker. The Blue Book says the order of unsaturation and chain length from earlier recommendations is reversed. So for CH2=C(CH2CH3)CH2CH2CH3 the six-carbon chain that leaves out the double bond is the parent (3-methylidenehexane), not the five-carbon chain that contains it (2-ethylpent-1-ene, the older name). The sentence also says any functional group must be in the parent, but only the principal (suffix) group must be. A prefix-only group such as an ether need not be. Core Concept repeats the double- and triple-bond claim: 'When a compound has a double bond, a triple bond or a main functional group, the parent must contain it.' The rule is right for the main functional group (Example 12 is correct). Many school texts still teach the 1979/1993 order, so the lead may need to rule on which convention to keep. As written, the lesson calls a current IUPAC name wrong.
findings.source: IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Chemistry, Recommendations 2013 (Blue Book), P-44.3 (the greater number of skeletal atoms is senior), P-44.4.1.1 and P-46.1 (the seniority of unsaturation and chain length from earlier recommendations is reversed), iupac.qmul.ac.uk/BlueBook/P4.html, accessed 2026-11-03; checklist B01; reader-rules boundary test (Sol audit)

findings.quote: The longest chain is not always the parent. For example, the group $-OH$ makes an alcohol
findings.problem: This Core Concept paragraph has five sentences, and the guide allows one to three. The paragraph that starts 'An aldehyde and a ketone with the same atoms' has four sentences. So does the first Speed Tricks paragraph, which starts 'For a hydrocarbon family'.
